summary: Proposes a Telnet option that lets a client control a serial port on a remote device, for example to set the line speed. The goal is to make modems attached to a network usable for outbound dialing. It is an experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: It lets your computer reach across the network and use a modem plugged into a different computer, as if it were plugged into your own.

subtitle: Remote control of serial ports on network access servers.

tldr.problem: Network users need to reach modems and serial devices attached to remote access servers for outbound dialing and other serial communication, but standard Telnet does not provide a way to configure the serial port settings.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2217 defines a new Telnet option (option 44) that allows a client to send commands to an access server to configure COM port parameters like baud rate, data size, parity and stop bits, and to control signals like BREAK, DTR and RTS.
tldr.outcome: The protocol remains experimental and sees limited deployment, but it enables network-based modem dialing and serial device control through Telnet sessions.

today: RFC 2217 is an Experimental protocol and remains experimental. It has not been obsoleted and defines a working option for serial port control over Telnet, though deployment is limited.

sections.title: Using Serial Devices Over the Network
sections.content:
RFC 2217 adds a new capability to Telnet: the ability to control a serial (COM) port on a remote device. The typical use case is an access server—a device on a network that has both a Telnet interface and one or more serial ports connected to modems or other serial devices. A client can establish a Telnet session to the access server and send configuration commands to set up the serial port, then communicate with a modem or other serial device connected to that port.

This is useful for scenarios such as dialing into the internet through a remote modem, connecting to bulletin board systems, accessing databases, or sending and receiving faxes over a dial-up connection. The RFC defines both the negotiation protocol and the specific commands to configure and monitor the serial port.
sections.plainLanguage: A Telnet command lets you tell a computer far away what settings to use on its modem, and to hear back when the modem picks up a call.

sections.title: Client, Access Server and the Modem
sections.content:
The architecture has three parts: a client (the user's computer), an access server (a network device with a Telnet interface and serial ports), and a remote service (such as an ISP, bulletin board or fax machine). The client connects to the access server via Telnet over the network. The access server relays data between the Telnet session and a serial port. The modem (or other serial device) on that port connects to the remote service.

The option uses Telnet's standard negotiation mechanism: the client sends IAC WILL COM-PORT-OPTION (option code 44) to indicate it wants to send port control commands, and the access server sends IAC DO COM-PORT-OPTION to accept them. Once negotiated, the client can send configuration and control commands in the form of Telnet subnegotiation (IAC SB ... IAC SE) packets.
sections.plainLanguage: You talk to the access server over Telnet, it talks to the modem through a cable, and the modem talks to the far-away computer. The option lets you shout instructions to the access server about how to set up its modem.

sections.title: Configuration Commands
sections.content:
The RFC defines commands to set serial port parameters. The client sends IAC SB COM-PORT-OPTION SET-BAUD <value> IAC SE to set the baud rate; the value is four octets representing the baud rate in bits per second (0 requests the current setting). The SET-DATASIZE command sets the number of data bits (5, 6, 7, or 8). The SET-PARITY command chooses NONE, ODD, EVEN, MARK or SPACE parity. The SET-STOPSIZE command selects 1, 1.5, or 2 stop bits.

Each configuration command sent by the client must be acknowledged by the access server with the actual value set. This matters because the access server may not support the requested value (for example, a client may request a baud rate faster than the hardware allows). The RFC recommends sending configuration commands in order: baud rate, then data size, parity and stop size, since some combinations are invalid (for example, EVEN parity with 8 data bits).
sections.plainLanguage: You send a command saying 'set the speed to 9600 bits per second' and the modem box writes back saying 'OK, it is now 9600'.

sections.title: Control Signals and Flow Control
sections.content:
Beyond configuration, the RFC defines SET-CONTROL commands to manage special signals. These include BREAK (send a serial break condition), DTR (Data Terminal Ready), and RTS (Request to Send). Each can be requested (to query the current state), set ON, or set OFF. The RFC also supports flow control modes: no flow control, XON/XOFF, or hardware (RTS/CTS) flow control. These can be set separately for inbound and outbound traffic.

The access server can notify the client of changes in the serial line state (data ready, parity error, framing error, break detected) and modem state (carrier detect, ring indicator, data-set-ready). The client sets bit masks to control which notifications it receives. The RFC also defines PURGE-DATA to flush receive or transmit buffers, and flow control commands (FLOWCONTROL-SUSPEND and FLOWCONTROL-RESUME) to pause transmission during the Telnet session itself.
sections.plainLanguage: You can tell the modem to hang up (drop DTR), detect when someone calls (carrier detect), or pause the stream of data if your computer gets overwhelmed.

sections.title: Security and Session Management
sections.content:
The RFC notes that authentication should be handled using existing Telnet authentication methods, such as Kerberos (RFC 1411) or SPX authentication (RFC 1412). More importantly, when a Telnet session ends, the access server should reset the COM port to a factory or administrator-defined configuration. This ensures the port is in a known state and ready for the next client session, preventing the modem or device from being left in an unexpected configuration that could cause problems or security issues.

The specification does not define any special encryption or further security mechanisms beyond what Telnet already provides; security relies on existing authentication and administrative controls on the access server.
sections.plainLanguage: Make sure only the right people can use the modem, and always put the settings back to normal when someone disconnects.
